Vote 279, Indian Education: Coal purchased for Bersimis Day School


AUDITOR GENERAL'S OFFICE, November 5, 1924.

SIR, - Education cheque No. 2755 of 1923 - 24 is for the payment of $228 to Louis Verreault & Son, of Petits Mechins
for 10 tons of coal, in sacks, for the Bersimis Day School. Cheque No. 4416 of the same year is for a payment of
$524.32 to Madden & Son of Quebec for 26.09 tons coal in sacks, also for the Bersimis Day School.

So far as I can gather from the accounts received at this office the Bersimis school was closed during the fall and
winter of 1923 - 24, a new combined boarding and day school being in process of erection, which was completed
about the beginning of February, 1924.

I should like to be informed whether this coal, or any part of it, was used for heating the new building while it was in
the contractor's hands, or if it was purchased before the close of navigation for the sole purpose of heating the building
after it was taken over from the contractor.

The cost of the coal includes 547 sacks at 10 cents and 126 at 15 cents, amounting to $72.70. Kindly let me know if
these sacks were returnable on repayment, or if not what disposition was made of them.


I am, sir, your obedient servant,

<!-- page 576 -->
WM. KEARNS, Asst. A.G.


The Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, Ottawa.



=== EXTRACT FROM HERE (pages 577-580) ===
<!-- page 577 -->
DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS, November 11, 1924.

SIR, - I have your letter of the 5th instant, regarding the payments made for the coal supplied the Bersimis Indian. Day
School during 1923 - 24.

While the classroom activities at this school were not carried on during the fall and winter of that year, owing to the
erection of a new combined day school and teachers' residence, it was necessary after the building was taken over
from the contractor that fire be kept going at all times during the winter, in order to prevent the heating and water
system from freezing and also damage to the building.

The coal has to be delivered in sacks, as this is the only way it can be handled owing to the difficulty in unloading at
Bersimis. This coal has to be handled several times between the point of shipment and the school. I am informed by
our engineer, who is familiar with the conditions, that the sacks are useless for further service by the time the coal is
delivered in the bins. As a consequence, they are not returned, and therefore a refund for the amount charged is not
obtainable.


Yours very truly,
D.C. SCOTT, D.S.G.


The Assistant Auditor General.

Vote 279, Indian Education: Suggesting Separate Appropriation for Erection or Purchase of New Schools


AUDITOR GENERAL'S OFFICE, May 23, 1924.

SIR, - Section 9 of the Public Works Act provides that the Minister of Public Works shall have the management,
charge and direction of the following properties belonging to Canada: (d) The public buildings.

Section 10 provides that nothing in section 9 shall be deemed to confer upon the Minister of Public Works the
management, charge or direction of such public works as are (c) by or under the authority of this Act or of any other
Act of the Parliament of Canada, placed under the control and management of any other minister or department.

Section 35 provides that the Governor in Council may at any time transfer the management, charge and direction of
any public work, or any power, duty or function with respect to any work or class of works, which is assigned to, or
vested by statute in any minister or department, to any other minister or department.

As I have been unable to find anything in the Indian Act which can be interpreted as conferring upon the
Superintendent General of Indian Affairs the management, charge or direction of the buildings erected for or occupied
by the Department of Indian Affairs, I am of the opinion that under Section 9 the management, etc., of such buildings
is with the Minister of Public Works unless formally transferred to the Superintendent General by the Governor in
Council in accordance with section 35.

On March 23rd, 1923, I wrote you suggesting that in future, when preparing your estimates, you ask for separate votes
(1) for the maintenance of existing schools and (2) for the erection or purchase of new schools; to which letter you
replied on March 26th that careful consideration would be given to that suggestion. I find, however, on examining the
estimates submitted to parliament for the current fiscal year that my suggestion was not acted upon.

As there thus appears to be no statutory authority for your department making any expenditure on account of the
erection or maintenance of the buildings and as no formal transfer under the provisions of section 35 appears

1 - 14r

<!-- page 578 -->

<!-- page 579 -->
at any time to have been made I am of the opinion that the practice of your department of making such expenditure is
contrary, to the provisions of the Public Works Act, and I have to ask that you se ek to obtain the necessary authority
to permit of your incurring such expenditure in future.


I am, sir, your obedient servant,
G. GONTHIER, A.G.


The Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs.


DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS, June 7, 1924.

DEAR SIR, - I have to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 23rd of May.

Your suggestion that when preparing our estimates we should ask for separate votes (1) for the maintenance of existing
schools, and (2) for the erection or purchase of new schools, was, I regret to say, overlooked, but I am asking my Chief
Accountant to take note that the estimates should be prepared in this manner for next year.


Yours very truly,
D.C. SCOTT, D.S.G.


The Auditor General.

Casual Revenue: Transfer of Yacht "Roamer" to Royal Military College, for Consideration of one Dollar


AUDITOR GENERAL'S OFFICE, November 24, 1924.

SIR, - Among the amounts deposited by your department to the credit of Casual Revenue during the fiscal year 1923 -
24 I find an amount of $1, deposited on June 7th, 1923, as having been received from the Commandant of the Royal
Military College, Kingston, on account of the purchase price of the yacht Roamer.

This boat was, I find, purchased by your department during the fiscal year 1918 - 19, for the use of Inspector
C.C. Parker, at the cost of $3,000.

As there is such a striking difference between the original cost of the boat and the merely nominal sum for which it
was transferred to, the Royal Military College, I have to ask for the full particulars connected with the use of this boat
and with its transfer to the Military authorities. I have also to ask if any special authority was obtained for the transfer.


I am, sir, your obedient servant,
WM. KEARNS, Asst. A.G.


The Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs.


DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS, November 26, 1924.

<!-- page 580 -->
SIR, - In reply to your letter of the 24th instant respecting the yacht Roamer, I have to say that it was transferred to the
Dominion Parks Branch of the Department of the Interior in October, 1920, and that Department transferred it, through
the Purchasing Commission of Canada, to the Royal Military College, Kingston. On the 26th June, 1923, the Dominion
Parks Branch of the Department of the Interior wrote this Department as follows: -
